title: Assisted Living Marketing: How to Fill Rooms With Ads (2026)
summary: Assisted living marketing for community directors: what the ads that keep running show, sample copy, lead channels, and how to track cost per move-in.
body_markdown:
## The short answer


- Assisted living marketing is aimed at the adult child, not the resident. Write for a tired, worried daughter or son who is searching at night and wants to feel the decision is safe.
- The ads that keep running name the community and the place, show the apartments and amenities, and send people to learn more or book a private tour.
- Best channels: Google Search for people already looking, Meta (Facebook and Instagram) for the family still deciding, a complete Google Business Profile, and referral partners.
- Measure cost per tour and cost per move-in, not clicks. One move-in is worth many months of rent.


## Who assisted living marketing is really written for


A resident rarely starts the search. An adult child does, often after a fall, a hospital discharge or a hard phone call. That person is worn out, a little guilty and short on time. They are not shopping for amenities first. They want to know whether this place is safe, whether it is close, and whether they can see it this week.


That changes how you write. Good assisted living advertising reassures first and sells second. It makes the next step small, such as a private tour or a call to a real person, and it avoids pressure.


Adult child Resident Referral source


Role Starts the search and often makes the call Has a say, often late in the process Hospital discharge planner, physician office, elder law attorney, placement advisor


What they want Safety, location, a staff they trust, reassurance Independence, dignity, a place that feels like home A community that answers fast and takes the handoff seriously


Where you reach them Google Search, Facebook, Instagram, your website Mostly through the tour and family conversations Direct outreach, lunches, visits, a short one-page summary


Best next step Private tour or a call A meal or an afternoon visit A quick availability check by phone


## What the live assisted living ads show


The[assisted living ad wall](https://www.sprites.ai/assisted-living-ads) shows 46 live Meta ads from 12 advertisers. A few patterns stand out.


- **Most ads are images, not video.** About 7% are video. Communities in this set are running photos of the building, rooms and grounds.
- **The ads run for a long time.** The median ad has been live 107 days. The longest-running ones have been up for 1,129 days, more than three years. These are not ads that get swapped every week.
- **The common button is Learn more.** About 43% of the ads use it. It asks for little and sends the family to the community's own site.
- **The long runners lead with the community name and place.** One opens with "Elevate Your Senior Living Experience in Vermont". Another says "Discover life at" the community, then promises apartment styles and amenities. Another says the community is redefining senior living "with care and compassion."


What they have in common is plain. They name where the community is, they show what living there looks like, and they ask for an easy next step. They do not rely on a discount or a clever hook, and that is probably why they can run for years.


The ads that fill rooms usually add three things on top of that: a private tour offer, a direct phone line a family can reach a person on, and one line of reassurance from a real family, such as a daughter saying her mother is thriving. Use a family quote only with written permission.


## What Meta's health rule means for these ads


Meta does not let health ads assert or imply anything about the viewer's own health, so "Struggling with memory loss?" gets rejected where "Memory care community near you" runs. Write about the community and its services, and never about the person looking at the ad.


## Assisted living advertisement examples


Below are sample lines you can adapt. Replace the town, the names and the numbers with your own. Use only claims you can back up.


Element Weak version Stronger version


Headline Luxury senior living Assisted living in Glastonbury. Tour this week.


Image Stock photo of smiling seniors A real photo of a one-bedroom apartment or the dining room at lunch


Body Premier care for your loved one Private apartments, three meals a day, nurses on site. See where your parent would live.


Proof Award-winning "Mom is thriving here. We wish we had visited sooner." A daughter, with permission.


Action Contact us Book a private tour, or call Dana directly at (555) 010-0142


### Facebook and Instagram ad


**Image:** the front entrance or a bright apartment, taken in daylight. **Primary text:** "Visiting a community is easier than reading about one. Walk through our apartments, meet the care team and eat lunch with us. Tours are private and take about an hour." **Headline:** "Private tours of assisted living in \[Town\]." **Button:** Learn more or Book now.


### Google Search ad


Responsive search ads allow up to 15 headlines of 30 characters and 4 descriptions of 90 characters, per Google Ads Help. A starting set:


Element Copy Characters


Headline 1 Assisted Living in Glastonbury 30


Headline 2 Book a Private Tour 19


Headline 3 Memory Care Also Available 26


Headline 4 See Apartments and Pricing 26


Description 1 Private apartments, dining and 24-hour care staff. Call to schedule a tour. 75


Description 2 Talk with a real person today. Ask about availability and what is included. 75


Searchers using words like "assisted living near me" or "memory care in \[town\]" are already looking. Pricing transparency in the ad helps, because families are often afraid of surprise costs.


## Which channels bring assisted living leads


1. **Google Search.** The highest intent. Target the town and the surrounding area where families live, not just where the community is. Add the words "assisted living," "memory care" and "senior living" in separate ad groups so the ad matches the search.
2. **Google Business Profile.** Real photos, an accurate phone number, tour hours and reviews. Families read reviews closely, and a community with few of them looks risky.
3. **Facebook and Instagram.** Adult children are on both. Use these to stay in front of families still deciding, with tour offers and photos of daily life. For how other health-adjacent businesses handle the wording rules, see[Facebook ads for med spas](https://www.sprites.ai/facebook-ads-for-med-spas) and[chiropractic marketing](https://www.sprites.ai/chiropractic-marketing) .
4. **Retargeting.** Many families visit your site, leave, and come back weeks later. A short follow-up ad with the community name and a tour button keeps you in mind.
5. **Referral partners.** Hospital discharge planners, elder law attorneys and placement advisors send move-ins. This is relationship work and it pays back slowly and steadily.
6. **Your website.** Every ad lands here. Put the phone number at the top, show a floor plan, state what is included in rent, and make the tour form short.


For broader ideas that carry across local businesses, see[local business ads](https://www.sprites.ai/local-business-ads) .


## The math from lead to move-in


Assisted living has a long, human sales cycle, so count the whole path. Here is a worked example. Replace each number with your own.


Step Example number Result


Monthly ad spend $3,000


Cost per lead $100 30 leads


Leads who book a tour 40% 12 tours


Tours that become move-ins 25% 3 move-ins


Cost per move-in $3,000 divided by 3 $1,000


Now compare that with what a resident is worth. If monthly rent is $5,500 and the average stay is 22 months, one move-in brings in about $121,000. A $1,000 cost per move-in looks small against that. A $10,000 cost per move-in may still make sense. The point is to know your number before you judge a channel.


The weak link is often not the ad. If 30 leads produce only 5 tours, the problem is speed and follow-up. Families who call or fill out a form expect an answer the same day. Check how fast your team returns calls before you raise the budget.


## Creative checklist for assisted living advertising


- Name the community and the town in the first line.
- Use real photos of apartments, dining and common rooms, not stock images.
- Write to the adult child, in plain words.
- Offer a private tour as the main action.
- Put a direct phone line in the ad or on the landing page, with a person's name if you can.
- Add one line of family reassurance, with permission.
- Never write about the viewer's own health or a relative's condition in the ad copy.
- Leave ads running long enough to learn from them. The ads on the wall run for months and years, not days.

## FAQ


### What is the best assisted living marketing strategy?


Start with Google Search and a complete Google Business Profile to catch families who are already looking. Add Meta ads that show your community and offer a private tour. Build referral relationships with discharge planners and elder law attorneys. Track cost per tour and cost per move-in.


### How do I get more assisted living leads?


Make it easy to take the next step. Show real photos, name the town, publish what is included in rent, and offer a private tour with a direct phone line. Then answer every lead the same day. Many communities lose leads through slow follow-up, not weak ads.


### Do Facebook ads work for assisted living communities?


Yes, for reaching adult children before they search. The ads on the[assisted living ad wall](https://www.sprites.ai/assisted-living-ads) are mostly images that name the community and invite families to learn more. Write about the community, not the viewer's health, because Meta rejects health ads that assert or imply something about the person seeing them.


### How long should an assisted living ad run?


Longer than most owners expect. The median ad on the wall has run 107 days, and the longest have run more than three years. Families take weeks or months to decide, so give an ad time to build results before you replace it.


### How much should an assisted living community spend on advertising?


Work backward from a move-in. Estimate what a resident is worth over an average stay, decide how much of that you can spend to win one, then divide by your tour and move-in rates to find how many leads you need and what you can pay for each.
